KEY MESSAGE 1...
A more active pattern is on the horizon beginning later 
Saturday evening and continuing through next week. A breakdown 
of the southeastern CONUS ridging will open the door for rounds 
of waves embedded within quasi-zonal flow and associated rain.

Round one arrives late Saturday and continues into Sunday as an 
initial mid-level wave rides along a baroclinic zone through the 
Ohio Valley. Ongoing convection Saturday morning poses an 
interesting evolution into the evening hours as CAMs attempt to 
handle the previously poorly modeled extent. Warm starts are now 
capturing it better and suggest that outflow extends as far south as 
south-central Illinois, sparking additional development there. This 
is progged to track east through the afternoon and arrive into our 
eastern Ohio counties just around dark. This should point toward 
weakening, and the 12z suite of CAMs suggests that, though maybe not 
quite to the extent that they think as point soundings ahead of it 
still show some elevated instability. The severe threat should be 
low provided the timing is correct, but lingering showers and 
rumbles of thunder are certainly in the cards, especially for the 
southwestern part of our area where the storms should be diving 
toward the best instability axis during the day. Farther north, 
ongoing warm advection and low-level jet driven showers likely 
continue as the broad ascent spreads east. While light as drier 
lower levels on our 12z balloon need saturated, the expectation is 
scattered light showers within mostly cloudy and cooler air.

Another push of precip, this one likely a bit more widespread and 
moderate to heavy at times, arrives Sunday morning as another wave 
rides atop the surface boundary. This time, a more prolonged 
period of southerly flow on the warm side is able to bring HREF 
mean PWAT values up to 1.6-1.9" and near the 99th percentile of 
climatology. A deep, saturated column with fumes of 100-300 J/kg
of MUCAPE within the warm cloud layer should be supportive of 
efficient rainfall rates. That said, it likely will take 
repeated rounds of heavy rain over the same area to raise flash 
flood concerns as mean cloud bearing layer wind is around 30 
knots, and HREF prob of 1" in an hour in any given hour tomorrow
doesn't reach much above 20-30% thus supporting the lower 
probability of intense rainfall rates but rather longer duration
totals to monitor. There are higher pockets of 50-60% 
probability for >1" in 24 hours. The deep column moisture should
offset a severe threat with limited instability. 

Following a brief lowering of rain chances early Monday, it'll 
remain active into the middle part of the week. While the setup 
doesn't appear to favor heightened flash flooding concerns any given 
day, long duration accumulation has the potential to be more 
notable. Latest NBM 48 hour QPF from Monday morning - Wednesday 
morning has the highest values south of Pittsburgh where a slow 
moving/stalled boundary is progged to be. Location of that will be 
paramount for who gets the bulk of the rain, and right now, most 
ensembles place it south of Pittsburgh. Mean values are around 1.25-
1.5" there, and 90th percentile values up to 2-3.5". Farther north, 
the mean is much less at 0.5-0.75" with the high end around 1.5-2". 
There are even some solutions (mostly a southward displaced 
boundary) in which the northern part of the area sees very 
little rain. While this all told wouldn't pose as much a threat 
for flash flooding, areal flooding and river flooding chances 
may increase especially if the high-end potential is realized. 
The primary way to realize that high end potential would be to 
be positioned immediately north of the stationary boundary with 
overrunning, and/or on the northwest side of a developing 
coastal low. Should the stationary boundary be too far south or 
the coastal low to far east, these threats would not be 
realized. The area with highest potential for impacts will be 
south of Pittsburgh and will need continued monitoring into 
early week.

KEY MESSAGE 2...
The other story of the week is going to be the much cooler air 
in place with several days where the highs may not get out of 
the 50s for some. Surface high pressure across New England will 
induce stout, prolonged east-northeast flow locally. NBM probs 
for daytime highs exceeding 65F is basically a 50/50 shot from 
the ridges to Pittsburgh, then a bit higher farther west, all 
that with a summertime-biased NBM and likely a bit too high even
at that; AI guidance and some deterministic models are running 
a handful of degrees cooler. Normal highs are in the low 70s and
lows in the low 50s throughout next week, so while lows should 
be right around normal, we could be looking at highs some 10 
degrees below.
